projectOutComesReport:
We are pleased to share the outcomes of our National Science Foundation (NSF) funded project, "RAPID: A Novel Detector for Mitigating the Covid-19 Pandemic based on Phase Interrogated Ultra-sensitive Microwave Resonance." This project aimed to develop an innovative breath analyzer, known as the Open-Ended Hollow Coaxial Cable Resonator (OE-HCCR), to revolutionize pulmonary function testing. Our work addresses both the intellectual merit and broader impacts of scientific research, with implications for healthcare and diagnostics.

Project Overview: Our research centered on the development of a noninvasive, real-time breath analyzer capable of distinguishing between healthy and compromised lung functions. Traditional pulmonary function tests can be expensive and complex, limiting their accessibility. To overcome these challenges, we introduced the OE-HCCR breath analyzer, a breakthrough in exhaled breath condensate analysis.

Key Findings and Outcomes:

  1. Innovation in Diagnostics: The OE-HCCR breath analyzer leverages electromagnetic analysis of exhaled breath components to detect subtle abnormalities. We successfully demonstrated its heightened sensitivity to nonvolatile particulate matter, such as virus particles, indicative of compromised lung function.

  2. Cost-Effective Healthcare Tool: Our research yielded a cost-effective and reliable diagnostic tool that holds great promise for widespread adoption in diverse healthcare settings. The OE-HCCR analyzer is designed to enhance the accessibility of pulmonary assessments.

  3. Mathematical Model: We developed a comprehensive mathematical model to support the functionality of the breath analyzer, which was corroborated by experimental results. This model serves as a foundation for the technology's precision and accuracy.

  4. Experimental Validation: Our experiments involved five key studies, including the sensitivity of phase signals to various substances, material variations within the active cavity, and the influence of different breathing techniques. These experiments demonstrated the OE-HCCR analyzer's ability to distinguish between exhaled breath and ambient air, as well as its sensitivity to breath content.

  5. Breath Signal Analysis: We identified distinct patterns in breath signal profiles, with elongated signal tails indicating higher concentrations of nonvolatile materials. This observation has significant implications for the diagnosis of respiratory conditions.

Broader Impacts: The outcomes of our project extend beyond scientific merit. The development of the OE-HCCR breath analyzer has the potential to:

  • Improve Healthcare Accessibility: By offering a cost-effective and noninvasive method for preliminary lung function assessment, this technology can make healthcare more accessible, particularly in resource-limited or remote areas.

  • Early Disease Detection: The OE-HCCR analyzer's ability to detect compromised lung function early could aid in the early diagnosis of respiratory diseases and conditions, facilitating timely interventions.

  • Research Advancements: Our project contributes to the advancement of respiratory research, providing a valuable tool for researchers to study breath content in greater detail.

Future Directions: While our current focus has been on nonvolatile components in exhaled breath, we are actively exploring the analysis of volatile components. Future research endeavors include incorporating thin-film metal organic framework (MOF) structures within the active cavity to achieve specificity for specific volatile organic compounds. This could enable disease diagnosis and contagion determination.

Conclusion: The NSF-funded project, "RAPID: A Novel Detector for Mitigating the Covid-19 Pandemic based on Phase Interrogated Ultra-sensitive Microwave Resonance," has resulted in the development of a groundbreaking breath analyzer with far-reaching implications for healthcare and diagnostics. The OE-HCCR breath analyzer offers a cost-effective and accessible solution for preliminary lung function assessment, with the potential to improve healthcare outcomes and advance our understanding of respiratory health.

We are grateful to the NSF for their support throughout this project, and we look forward to further developments and applications of our innovative technology in the field of healthcare and beyond.

abstractText:
NON-TECHNICAL ABSTRACT
Unlike line-of-sight propagation in a translucent medium, light transport in an opaque medium is a seemingly random walk that is described by a diffusion process. Common to electronic, acoustic, as well as the electromagnetic waves, most of the incident wave is reflected, and only a small fraction is transmitted via a multitude of partial waves with a broad range of delay times. Counterintuitively, this behavior can be altered by exploiting wave interference. This award supports an experimental and theoretical efforts to investigate the degree, to which one can manipulate input waves in a chip-scale platform, to achieve near-100% transmission or avoid temporal spread of a short pulse. The collaborative program of an experimental group at Yale University and a theoretical group at Missouri University of Science & Technology will train graduate and undergraduate students to conduct interdisciplinary research across the evolving boundaries of multiple fields, including condensed matter physics, optics of complex media, nanotechnology, and computational physics. The cutting-edge research will be incorporated in the curriculum at both participating institutions. This project includes an extensive exchange program with visits by faculty and students, summer internships, design and assembly of optical demonstrations for undergraduate research projects and recruitment activities.

TECHNICAL ABSTRACT
The concept of transmission eigenchannels has been a cornerstone of mesoscopic physics but it is also applicable to electromagnetic waves and acoustic waves. Despite of the essential role of the eigenchannels in mesoscopic transport and vast opportunities for optical/acoustic imaging applications, little is known about the intrinsic properties of individual transmission eigenchannels or the time-delay eigenchannels. This collaborative program supports a joint experimental and theoretical studies on the statistical properties of individual eigenchannels, such as their fluctuations and correlations, in a unique on-chip photonic platform that allows both selective coupling of light into a single eigenchannel and direct probe of its spatial structure inside the random medium. Compared to electronic systems, robustness of coherence effects for photons at room temperature makes optical systems ideal for the in-depth fundamental studies of coherent wave transport. The proposed work addresses long-standing questions in mesoscopic physics regarding the nature and statistical properties of individual transmission and time-delay eigenchannels and the roles they play in static and dynamic wave transport. A systematic comparison between the experimental and numerical results will provide key insights into how the eigenchannels are formed, what determines their properties, and whether it is possible to achieve simultaneously spatial and temporal control of wave transmission. The research program will produce a wide range of experimental and numerical data, which will pave the way for the mesoscopic physics community to develop and verify new theoretical models for coherent wave transport. In optics, the fundamental understanding of coherent propagation via eigenchannels will inform a broad range of practical applications, from laser surgery, photovoltaics, imaging in turbid media, to random laser and energy-efficient ambient lighting. The collaborative experimental-theoretical program will train graduate and undergraduate students to conduct interdisciplinary research across the evolving boundaries of multiple fields, including condensed matter physics, optics of complex media, nanotechnology, and computational physics. The cutting-edge research will be incorporated in the curriculum at both participating institutions. The two teams will join force in education outreach activities.

projectOutComesReport:
This collaborative research project between Missouri University of Science and Technology and Yale University has made groundbreaking advances in fundamental understanding and experimental control of how light and other waves travel through complex materials like biological tissue or fog. Imagine trying to shine a flashlight through your hand - the light scatters in all directions, making it difficult to control where the energy goes. The research has developed new methods to shape light waves so one can, for example, deliver energy to specific locations deep inside scattering materials.

The initial breakthrough was the discovery that special waves patterns traveling through disordered materials, so called transmission eigenchannels, exhibit unexpected correlations in their transmission properties. This finding led to the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for predicting how waves behave in complex materials. Building on this foundation, the research team discovered “deposition eigenchannels” - special wave patterns that can concentrate light at desired depths inside complex scattering media. They demonstrated that light intensity at the target can be enhanced up to six times compared to conventional methods, even when using broadband light (light containing many colors). They also introduced “remission eigenchannels” that significantly improve the ability to detect signals coming from deep inside materials. These capabilities have important implications for medical imaging, phototherapy, and other applications requiring precise energy delivery through tissue.

Another major breakthrough was the first conclusive demonstration of “Anderson localization” of light in three dimensions - a phenomenon predicted over 40 years ago but never definitively observed. This discovery helps explain how waves can become trapped in disordered materials, with implications for both fundamental physics and practical applications in photonics and electronics.

The broader impacts of this work extend across multiple fields:

  • Medical Applications: These techniques could improve non-invasive diagnostic imaging and light-based therapies
  • Telecommunications: Better understanding of wave propagation could lead to improved signal transmission
  • Renewable Energy: More efficient light delivery could enhance solar cells and photocatalysis
  • Education: The project trained students in cutting-edge research methods, preparing them for careers in science and technology

Beyond specific technical achievements, this project has established new fundamental principles for controlling waves in complex media. The mathematical frameworks and experimental techniques developed here provide a foundation for future advances in fields ranging from condensed matter physics, optics, acoustics, biomedical imaging to telecommunications. 

The collaboration has produced multiple high-impact publications in prestigious journals including Nature Physics, Nature Photonics, Physical Review Letters and Proceedings of the National Academy of Scince, while fostering international cooperation between researchers in the United States, France, and Turkey. The developed light scattering demonstration and hands-on experiments have been used to engage middle- and high-school students at the annual outreach events at Missouri S&T. The project has also contributed to training and mentoring the next generation of scientists, with students and researchers continuing on to successful careers in academia and industry.

abstractText:
This award supports participation of early-career researchers in the annual conference "The Midwest Numerical Analysis Day" held at the campus of Missouri University of Science and Technology, Rolla, MO, on September 25-26, 2020. The Midwest Numerical Analysis Day has provided a forum since the 1990s for computational mathematicians in the Midwest area to share their research on numerical methods and their analysis. Since many engineers will participate in the Midwest Numerical Analysis Day 2020, this conference will provide an important platform for computational scientists and engineers to communicate with each other on recent development, analysis, and applications of various numerical methods, and find common interests for future collaborations. The Midwest Numerical Analysis Day has also served as a yearly regional conference to provide an opportunity for graduate students and postdocs to present their research on numerical methods. 

The topics of this conference focus on the algorithm development, analysis, and applications of efficient, accurate, and stable numerical methods, especially those for solving multi-physics and multi-scale problems. In recent years, the inherent multi-physics and multi-scale features of many sophisticated and challenging real-world problems accentuate the importance to develop more efficient, accurate, and stable numerical methods for the relevant partial differential equations. In order to address these needs, the Midwest Numerical Analysis Day 2020 intends to create a forum for early-career and senior researchers from different fields, including computational mathematics, computer science, physics, and various engineering fields, to discuss recent advances on relevant numerical methods with the corresponding numerical analysis and applications.

projectOutComesReport:
Midwest Numerical Analysis Day 2021 was hosted at Havener center of Missouri University of Science and Technology from October 29-30, 2021. This NSF grant was used to provide travel support to 11 graduate students and 1 postdoc for attending the conference and giving presentations. This conference is featured with 4 plenary presentations, 50 parallel presentations in 12 parallel sessions, and 116 participants.

The Midwest Numerical Analysis Day conference series brings together young mathematicians, mathematics graduate students, recent PhDs, women and underrepresented groups into contact with a community of active researchers. The conference places an emphasis on helping junior researchers in the research areas of computational and applied mathematics to grow and develop, with a low-cost high-efficiency forum for the computational and applied mathematicians in the Midwest area.

Compared with the previous Midwest Numerical Analysis Day meetings, more engineers attended this meeting. In order to provide a forum for the scientists and engineers to communicate with each other for possible future collaborations, we have two engineers (one in academia and one in industrial) in the local organizing committee and invite many engineers to present their numerical works and applications.

A special issue for this conference will be published on International Journal of Numerical Analysis and Modeling for this conference. Missouri Institute for Computational and Applied Mathematical Sciences is being expanded at Missouri University of Science and Technology.  Funding for this project supported the growth of this institute and enhanced the relatively small amount of computational mathematics research activities in the state of Missouri.

This award is to assist US-based students to attend the 2020 IEEE International Conference on Pervasive Computing and Communications (PerCom) to be held in Austin, Texas, March 23-27, 2020. Participation in PerCom 2020 and similar conferences are valuable and important activities of the graduate school experience. It provides students with the opportunity to interact with more senior researchers, and exposes students to leading work and practical industry practices in this important area of research.  This may have an important impact on career development.

The conference spans five days and will consist of technical paper presentations, panels, industry presentations, posters, and demonstrations.  It will also feature keynote speeches from leading researchers and practitioners in the field.  

Student travel to conferences is an important activity. Funds will be dispersed with preference given to students who would not otherwise be able to attend the conference and paying particular attention to diversity and relevance of the student's research interest.

projectOutComesReport:
The IEEE International Conference on Pervasive Computing and Communications (PerCom) is a flagship conference in the area of pervasive computing and networking dealing with internet of things, cyber-physical systems, and smart systems (e.g., smart city, smart energy, smart healthcare, etc.). The NSF travel funds helped support 9 U.S. based students to attend IEEE PerCom in 2020 conference held virtually on March 23-27, 2020 and 23 U.S. based students attend IEEE PerCom 2021 conference held virtually on March 22-26, 2021 respectively (www.percom.org). More than a dozen of these students were women and six were under-represented minority students. They consisted of a mix of B.S., M.S. and Ph.D. students from smaller schools to big name schools.

 

Intellectual Merit: Papers presented at the IEEE PerCom 2020 and PerCom 2021 conferences were very high quality. The technical programs included a wide variety of topics in pervasive computing and networking and emerging topics like smartphone sensing, mobile crowdsensing, smart city, security and social networks with applications to cyber-physical-human systems, smart and connected communities, smart healthcare, internet of things (IoT), security, energy and sustainability. The conference offered a valuable opportunity for the supported U.S. based students to attend keynote talks and technical sessions, learn about state-of-the-art research in pervasive computing, systems and applications through paper presentations and panel discussions, and participate in the Ph.D. forum, workshops, demo, poster, and work-in-progress sessions. The students also got the opportunity to network with peers and top notch researchers in pervasive computing. They were highly motivated to pursue high quality research and eventually research careers upon graduation.

 

Broader Impacts. The NSF travel grant supported 18 students including women and under-represented minority students, to attend a flagship conference IEEE PerCom 2020 and PerCom 2021. The NSF travel grant opportunity was widely advertised that led to the selection of students competitively from an application pool of more than 60 students. Without NSF travel support, many of these students would not have otherwise attended this flagship conference.

abstractText:
In 2018, the Department of the Interior, in response to a Presidential Executive Order, listed 35 critical minerals whose unreliable supply poses risks to our nation's economy and defense. Subsequently, on June 4, 2019, the U.S. Department of Commerce released the report "A Federal Strategy to Ensure Secure and Reliable Supplies of Critical Minerals" that outlines several Calls to Action that, if executed, will reduce the vulnerability of the United States to critical mineral supply disruptions. This grant is in support of an interdisciplinary national two-day workshop that will bring together stakeholders from academia, industry, and government to comprehensively address these calls. Themed topical sessions will discuss the resilient supply of critical minerals from cross-disciplinary, convergent perspectives, including mining engineering, extractive metallurgy, separations, policy, and others. National leaders in their respective fields will give keynote presentations, followed by TED-type talks, panel discussions, and breakout sessions. The breakout sessions will be structured for interdisciplinary engagement, to provide a convergent perspective that includes economic, technical, social, and policy aspects. Research road maps will be created that reflect the cross-disciplinary nature of approaches required to enhance supply resilience. The workshop findings will be summarized and disseminated via a publically-available workshop report. The workshop will be held at the Missouri University of Science and Technology in Rolla, Missouri, on May 27-28, 2020, and will be followed by an optional field trip on May 29, 2019 that will highlight the critical mineral potential of the Midwestern USA. 

The workshop will help nurture a budding national community with expertise in critical mineral supply resilience, spanning academia, industry, and government. Travel grants, for students and early-career researchers in particular, will help build a community that spans generations and will enhance the workshop's lasting impact. The development of a healthy and active critical mineral community is vital to the national economy and security because the United States is currently import-reliant for 31 of the 35 commodities on the critical minerals list. This workshop will generate insights into how U.S. universities can meet the projected future demands for the nation's critical minerals workforce, particularly in rural areas which are most likely to contain undiscovered resources. Therefore, the workshop will provide a basis for helping rural workforce development.

projectOutComesReport:
On December 20, 2017, President Donald J. Trump issued the Executive Order 13817, A Federal Strategy to Ensure Secure and Reliable Supplies of Critical Minerals, which addressed the issue with the United States' heavy reliance on imports of certain materials that are vital to the U.S. economy and defense. Critical minerals are defined as (i) non-fuel mineral commodities that are essential to the economic and national safety of the United States with (ii) supply chains that are vulnerable to disruption and (iii) that serve an essential function in the manufacturing of a product that is significance to the national economy and safety.

In 2019, the Department of State fulfilled the 2017 Presidential Executive Order and published a list that identified 35 critical minerals (the newer 2022 list includes 50 elements and minerals). Subsequently, the U.S. Department of Commerce released the 2019 strategic report A Federal Strategy to Ensure Secure and Reliable Supplies of Critical Minerals. This report outlines six Calls to Action that, if executed, will reduce the vulnerability of the United States to critical mineral supply disruptions. These six Calls to Action are:

(1) Advance Transformational Research, Development, and Deployment Across Critical Mineral Supply Chains.

(2) Strengthen America's Critical Mineral Supply Chains and Defense Industrial Base.

(3) Enhance International Trade and Cooperation Related to Critical Minerals.

(4) Improve Understanding of Domestic Critical Mineral Resources.

(5) Improve Access to Domestic Critical Mineral Resources on Federal Lands and Reduce Federal Permitting Timeframes.

(6) Grow the American Critical Minerals Workforce.

In 2020, the Thomas J. O'Keefe Institute for Sustainable Supply of Strategic Minerals at Missouri University of Science and Technology (Missouri S&T) received funding from the National Science Foundation (NSF) to host a workshop to identify research needs associated with these Calls to Action. The workshop was initially planned for May 2020 on the Missouri S&T campus, Rolla, Missouri, USA. However, due to the global COVID-19 pandemic, the format of the workshop was changed to a virtual workshop series via ZOOM. The first virtual workshop was held on August 2-3, 2021, and attracted 158 registrants, including 108 registrants from academia (61 students), 30 registrants from government agencies, and 20 registrants from the private sector. The second virtual workshop was conducted on August 4-5, 2022, and had 346 registrants, including 171 registrants from academia (62 students), 88 registrants from government agencies, and 87 registrants from the private sector.

In breakout sessions during the first workshop several issues that limit critical mineral supply chain resilience in the United States were identified and associated research needs were formulated, including:

(1) Insufficient understanding of domestic critical minerals resources. To address this issue, workshop participants highlighted the need for (i) more geologic research to identify new and evaluate existing resources; and (ii) a qualitative and quantitative assessment of critical minerals that may be recovered as by/co-products from existing production streams.

(2) Technical limitations of current mineral processing and recycling technologies. To address this issue, workshop participants highlighted the need for (i) innovative mineral processing technologies, including more environmentally friendly chemicals/solvents, and (ii) automated recycling technologies for appliances and e-waste. Participants also highlighted the need for a centralized and simplified way to collect recyclable materials, and incentives for the public to participate in recycling.

(3) Long permitting processes for mining and mineral processing operations, with often unpredictable outcomes. To address this issue, workshop participants suggested the development of new critical mineral focused policies with faster processing times and more transparent / predictable decision-making processes.

(4) The negative public image of mining and mineral processing operations. To address this issue, workshop participants suggested to design public outreach / education initiatives and to include local communities into decision-making processes.

(5) Limited availability of a critical mineral workforce. To address this issue, workshop participants suggested an increased focus on critical mineral specific skill training in higher education institutions, and advanced training of the existing workforce.

The second workshop followed up on these issues with invited presentations by leading experts in their fields followed by discussion sessions. The goal of a planned 2023 hybrid virtual and in-person workshop is to further discuss the findings of the 2021 and 2022 workshops and to kickstart research collaborations among different stakeholders which was difficult during the pandemic years.

Teaching and conducting research in Science and Technology Studies within engineering and polytechnic universities poses significant challenges and offers substantial opportunities. This workshop explores these challenges and opportunities by drawing together STS researchers who work in these contexts from across the nation at Missouri University of Science & Technology's new Center for Science, Technology, and Society. The group will discuss big ideas for advancing Science and Technology Studies in engineering schools, strategies for developing Science and Technology Studies communities, cohorts, and research centers in these contexts, and ideas for increasing impacts in engineering environments. Workshop outcomes will include a set of archived and curated workshop sessions, a research report, articles in a leading Science and Technology Studies journals, and the creation of a national community of Science and Technology Studies scholars interested in these issues.

This workshop will bring together a diverse group of researchers in Science and Technology Studies to discuss the appropriate role of Science and Technology Studies in engineering and polytechnical universities, and to develop collective strategies for overcoming the potential challenges of working in these environments and for capitalizing on the potential benefits of doing so. The workshop structure will be informed by recent scholarly reviews of the state-of-the-field within Science and Technology Studies, and by the experiences of Science and Technology Studies researchers who have worked in engineering and polytechnical universities. The workshop will result in strategic plans for advancing the place and impact of Science and Technology Studies in technical universities, the creation of a community of Science and Technology Researchers interested in these issues, and in research reports and scholarly articles.

projectOutComesReport:
Thanks to support from NSF's Science and Technology Studies division, the Missouri University of Science and Technology in Rolla, Missouri, was able to host a one-day virtual workshop titled "The Futures of STS at Engineering and Technological Universities" on September 24, 2021. The goal of the project was to host a ground-breaking, influential workshop with leading STS thinkers and researchers, to help direct the field forward in the context of work on polytechnic and engineering-focused campuses. After being postponed twice due to COVID, the event was held virtually due to ongoing concerns about travel amid the pandemic. Fortunately, all but one of the original invited participants from 2019 were able to take part in the workshop.

The workshop included participant/presenters from twelve STEM-focused universities across the country as well as attendees from multiple universities and various ranks, from undergraduate students to a university chancellor. Hosted by Missouri S&T's Center for Science, Technology, and Society, the workshop spawned multiple new collaborations among participants, many of whom knew each other only by reputation. The workshop also served to raise the visibility of STS at Missouri S&T, especially among students, engineering faculty, and university administrators. 

The workshop succeeded in bringing together some of the country's most innovative STS scholars on engineering and polytechnic campuses to discuss what strategies lead to growth and intellectual/academic relevance in these environments. Various sessions explored what actions can be taken to ensure continued buy-in by administrators, increase student interest/engagement, and foster productive interdisciplinary collaborations, especially between STS researchers and engineering/science faculty.

Professional relationships initiated or strengthened by the workshop continue, and significant future published work related to STS at engineering and polytechnic campuses will have had its origin in this singular event.
